personas.persona: Maya, 16, Year 11 in Manchester. Picked "School & mates". Scrolls TikTok in bed, bails the second something feels like a PSHE lesson. Played 20 cards this session.

issues.problem: I picked "School & mates" but about half the feed was adult stuff. I got Sam the manager, Rosa aged 68, a foreign qualification that isn't recognised, Peugeot, drug errors on hospital wards, an 18-month work project, and drink-driving. Those are "all" cards, so the filter lets them through. Every time a card is about someone at work or a pensioner, I scroll. The young-only cards (school days, friendship hours, homework merits, guitar/skins) were the ones that actually felt like mine.
issues.fix: In the feed, when world = School & mates, rank audience:"young" cards first and cap "all" cards at 1 in 3. Also give "all" cards an optional per-world override (e.g. game.steps[i].young) so the scenario text can be swapped. At minimum, do the swaps in the issues below.

issues.problem: Step 1 has a 16-year-old called Maya (that's literally me, fine, a bit creepy but funny). Then I get Sam the manager and Rosa, 68, walking round a covered market. Step 3 is the step that teaches the backup-plan trick, and it's the one I'm least likely to care about. I got it wrong and still didn't care.
issues.fix: Replace step 2 with: scenario "Jay keeps meaning to reply to his mate's voice notes but forgets till midnight. Pick the plan." Options: "I'll be a better mate." (feedback unchanged in spirit), and best: "When I get on the bus home, then I'll reply to one voice note before opening TikTok." Replace step 3 with: scenario "Your plan: revise 10 min when you put your bag down. What should you add to protect it?" Best option: "If I'm at my mate's after school, then I'll do the 10 minutes on the bus with flashcards." Wrong options: "If I miss a day, I'll do 30 minutes tomorrow." and "Nothing will stop me." Keep the existing feedback for both.

issues.problem: In the result screenshot, the black score dot sits right on the "Will" label, so it reads "W●". The result is also a wall of text that tells me to work out my lowest score myself ("Look at your lowest score above: if it's Skill... if it's the Open door... if they tie..."). That's a maths puzzle, not a result. The 6-question quiz at the start is also the slowest card in the feed, and it's the first card I saw.
issues.fix: In app.js, offset the venn marker so it never overlaps the axis labels, or move the labels outside the circles. Have the app compute the lowest axis and show only that branch. For example, W result text: "The want is strong today. Your weakest pillar is {lowest}: {action}." Here action = "do one 5-minute practice rep" for Skill and "ask one person for the chance or the time this week" for Open door. Also don't serve a 6-question venn as the first card of a session. Start with an estimate or reveal card.

issues.problem: The right end says "Fast on small, slow on big", but every question is about a small choice (show, card, returns). If I answer fast on everything, it tells me I'm "slow where it matters". I was never asked about anything big, so the result feels made up. "Treat a menu like a marriage" is a decent hook, but the birthday-card rack and free returns are mum stuff.
issues.fix: Change the right label to "Quick on undoable choices". Change the top zone text to: "Today you move fast on choices you can undo. Nice. Before a big one-way choice (GCSE options, quitting a team), slow down on purpose." Swap Q2 for "Picking what to wear to a mate's party, I…" (Try on everything twice and still hate it / Try two, pick one / Grab something and go). Swap Q4 for "Choosing a pic to post, I…" (Edit 30 versions and still doubt it / Pick from my top 3 / Post one I like, I can delete it).

issues.problem: Step 2 jumps from a laptop to someone drink-driving home safely. For a 16-year-old it lands a bit like a scary assembly. It's also not a situation I'm in. Both scenarios are adult (buying a laptop, driving).
issues.fix: Replace step 2 with: scenario "Your mate doesn't revise at all, guesses on the mock, and gets a 7. Good decision?" Best: "No. A good grade doesn't fix a bad bet." with feedback "Right. They got lucky on the questions. Do it again in the real exam and the dice might not be so kind." Wrong: "Yes, it worked." with feedback "That's 'resulting': grading a choice by how it turned out. It teaches people to repeat lucky gambles." Change step 1 "second-hand laptop" to "second-hand phone".

issues.problem: 3 of 5 items are adult life: a qualification earned abroad, looking after family every evening, a club that only takes members' friends. The 11pm caring one is real for young carers, so keep that idea, but the rest made me feel like I was reading my mum's LinkedIn. It's also tagged "Bit deeper" while being the clearest idea in the session.
issues.fix: Replace "The qualification you earned abroad isn't recognised where you live now." with "The art GCSE you want to take clashes with Triple Science on the timetable." (right; why: "A timetable rule, not a flaw. Ask your head of year about other options or a different block."). Replace the club item with "The football team only trains at a ground two buses away and you've no lift." (right; why: "That's access. Ask about lift shares or a closer team, not more willpower."). Change the caring item to "You can only revise after 10pm because you look after your little brother every evening."

issues.problem: Good card, honestly the most "about me" one. But "you've already used around 70% of your school days together" hit a bit hard at 1am. The "Not a reason to panic" line comes after the gut-punch number. The next card shown was "weather, not climate", which helped, but that's luck. Also not everyone leaves at 16 vs 18 the same way (college/sixth form), so the 380 can feel wrong.
issues.fix: Reorder the explain so the warm line comes first: "About 380. Not a countdown to panic over, a reason to say yes to Friday's plan. A school year is roughly 190 days (UK; about 180 in the US), so two years is about 380. Moving to college at 16 instead? Then it's this year that counts." Delete the "70% already used" sentence.

issues.problem: Hook about cash vanishing is fun, and the follower-count item is the best bit. But the Peugeot item has a long explanation about Harari's example. Nobody my age knows Peugeot as anything but a car. Only 6 items, and the result "2 of 6. Here's the pattern." felt like a mark out of 6 from a teacher.
issues.fix: Replace the Peugeot item with "Your school's uniform rules" (left; why: "The blazer is real fabric. The rule that it must be worn exists because people agree to keep it, and it can be changed."). Add "A TikTok trend" (left; why: "Only exists while people keep doing it."). Change the low-score result heading from "2 of 6. Here's the pattern." to "Tricky one! Here's the trick." when the score is under half.

personas.verdict: Honestly, better than I expected. The ones built for my age actually got me. "90 hours to make a friend" made me feel less weird about not clicking with people at college yet. Rat farms in Hanoi is a fact I'd send to the group chat. Skins vs £8 season pass is literally my life. The quick reveals and number guesses are fast and hit like a "wait, what" moment. The tone never makes me feel stupid when I'm wrong. But I picked School & mates and still got managers, a 68-year-old, hospital drug errors and drink-driving, and every one of those is an instant swipe. The Venn quiz is slow and makes me do the maths on my own result, and it was my first card, which nearly lost me. The decision-speed quiz gave me a result about "big choices" it never asked about. Make the whole feed feel like the friendship card and I'd keep playing. Right now it's about half me and half my mum.

personas.persona: Radu, 44, engineering manager in Cluj. Tired, a bit burned out, English is my second language. I picked "Work" in the picker and want tools I can use with my team tomorrow, no fluff.

issues.problem: This card is tagged audience 'work', so it was served because I picked Work. But step 1 is a friend leaving you on read and posting a story, and step 2 is a group project due tomorrow, which is a student situation. Only step 3 is about work, and even that one says '(at work, or on a school project)'. For a manager it feels like I got the teenager version.
issues.fix: Step 1 scenario: 'A colleague hasn't answered your Slack message since morning, but you see them active in another channel. Before you ping again, you tell yourself…'. Options: (a) 'They're ignoring me. I must have annoyed them.' (keep the feedback, but change 'Posting takes five seconds' to 'A quick reply elsewhere takes five seconds'); (b, best) 'They're probably buried. I'll ask again after lunch with a clear deadline.'; (c) 'Fine. I'll stop including them.' Step 2 scenario: 'A colleague hasn't sent their section of the client report, and it's due tomorrow. Which thought helps most?' In option (b)'s feedback, replace '(illness, a shift at work, a crashed laptop)' with '(sick kid, an urgent incident, unclear brief)'. Step 3: delete '(at work, or on a school project)'.

issues.problem: The Work filter only removes cards written for other worlds. About half my 20 cards were audience 'all', and their examples come from school, family and hobbies: phones banned in schools (steelmanning), card packs and the group chat (doomscroll), guitar and a members-only club (opportunity-gap), rats plus a 'family or class' team task (sleep), and 'lesson or family task' (attention residue). The Work world does not feel like my world.
issues.fix: Add optional per-world override fields to the card schema, e.g. "worlds": {"work": {"hook": ..., "try_team": ..., "items": [...]}}, and have app.js merge game.items/scenario/try_team from worlds[selectedWorld] when present. Also rank audience:'work' cards before audience:'all' cards in the Work feed, at a ratio of at least 2:1.

issues.problem: The only scenario is a friend arguing about phones in schools. Steelmanning is one of the most useful tools for my architecture debates and my 1:1s, but the card never shows me that.
issues.fix: Step 1 scenario: 'In a design review, a senior dev says: "We should not migrate to microservices this year." You disagree. Which reply is a steelman?' Options: (a) 'So you're just afraid of new tech?' (strawman); (b, best) 'You're worried we'd spend a year on infrastructure instead of features, with a team that has never run distributed systems in production. Fair?'; (c) 'Everyone said the same about the cloud.' Step 2 best option: 'Say where you agree (the team has no ops experience), then share your concern about deploy times blocking three teams.' Change try_team's 'Pick a topic people disagree on' to 'Pick the open technical decision your team argues about most'.

issues.problem: In the screenshot, the black score dot covers the 'Will' label, so it reads 'W●'. The result text also makes me run an algorithm in my head ('look at your lowest score; if it's Skill do X, if Open door do Y, if they tie…'). The app already knows my scores (Skill 5, Open door 5, a tie), so it should just tell me what to do. The prompt examples (revising, an instrument) are also not work examples.
issues.fix: In app.js, place the venn marker outside the label's bounding box, or put the label above the circle. Compute the lowest axis and render only the matching sentence, e.g. for W with Skill=Open door: 'Your want is strong. Skill and Open door tie, so start with the door: ask one person for the time or the chance this week.' Change the prompt to 'Pick one goal (a work project, a certification, a hard conversation, getting fitter). Answer every line for that one goal.'

issues.problem: The orange 'NEXT' teaser at the bottom of a Work card points to cards from other worlds: after the WSO venn it showed 'A friend says I'm just not a speaker…'. It breaks the world I chose, and it is the first thing I see when I finish a card.
issues.fix: In app.js, pick the NEXT teaser card with the same audience filter the feed uses (audience === selectedWorld || audience === 'all', preferring selectedWorld). Use a related concept only if a card for it passes the filter; otherwise fall back to the next card in the filtered feed.

issues.problem: The fact is interesting, but in the Work feed it gives me nothing for my team. The try_team says 'as a family or class', and for a burned-out manager the useful message (protect sleep after a learning day) is missing.
issues.fix: Change try_team to: 'After a training day or workshop, skip the late team call. Next morning at stand-up, each person says one thing they learned yesterday and you see what stuck.' Add to the insight: 'So a late-night push after a learning day can cost you part of that day's learning.'

issues.problem: This is a good card for me, but the try_team ('meeting, lesson or family task') is generic. My real problem is Slack and on-call pings breaking deep work, and the card doesn't touch that.
issues.fix: Change try_team to: 'Agree one 90-minute no-ping block each morning for the team: status set to Focus, Slack notifications off, and only on-call can interrupt. Review after two weeks: did fewer tasks spill over?'

issues.problem: On the My map view (light theme), domain labels sit on top of nodes and each other ('Old Wisdom' cuts through a node, 'Thinking' overlaps an orange dot, 'Habits' overlaps 'Emotions' nodes). It looks messy and I can't tap the nodes under the labels.
issues.fix: Give the labels a semi-opaque background pill (e.g. background: var(--bg) at 85% opacity, 4px padding) and pointer-events:none, and offset each label to the outer edge of its cluster's centroid rather than the centre.

personas.verdict: The cards made for work are good, really. The 1:1 'diagnose the stall' card, the questions that test your hunch, and the six-week bill of quick fixes are things I can use in tomorrow's stand-up and 1:1s, and they are short and honest about the evidence. The problem is that I picked Work and still got about half the feed about friends on read, school phone bans, card packs, guitar and rats. Then the NEXT button sends me to 'a friend says'. The tone is kind, it never shames me, and the sources are careful. Fix the world filter and rewrite the three or four mixed cards, and this goes from 'nice' to 'I send it to my team leads'.

personas.persona: Elena, 68, retired literature teacher. Reads Seneca, Aristotle and Peterson; values depth, accuracy and respect for the reader; allergic to pop-psych oversimplification. Picked "Everyday life".

issues.problem: I chose 'Everyday life', yet the orange/purple 'NEXT' button at the bottom of cards sends me to cards written for other worlds. On useful-truth-people-person it offers 'Every status report says green. So why is your...' (map-territory-green-dashboard-choice, audience 'work'). On hedonic-adaptation-lottery-reveal it offers 'Same page, same night. Your mate remembers stuff...' (goal-directed-perception-burglar-choice, audience 'young'). The feed filter works, but this button ignores it. It feels as if the app forgot what I told it a minute earlier.
issues.fix: In app.js line 219, filter the related targets by world: change `(BY_CONCEPT[cid] || []).filter((id) => !sameStory(card, CARD[id]))` to `(BY_CONCEPT[cid] || []).filter((id) => inWorld(CARD[id]) && !sameStory(card, CARD[id]))`, and add `&& inWorld(CARD[id])` to the fallback `.find(...)` as well. If a concept has no in-world card, drop that target.

issues.problem: The 'Everyday life' world still speaks to a teenager. I got 'a mate's page pays you per edit', 'speaking up in class', 'Put on your trainers', 'Opening card packs in a game', 'Getting a face tattoo', 'revision', 'Your team won 3-1', 'You're lost in London' and 'Adults' #1 life regret is about school'. Twenty cards and not one example from a life after 50 (grandchildren, retirement, health routines, an old friendship, a library book group). The ideas are universal; the costume is not, and it tells an older reader she is a guest here.
issues.fix: Give every audience:'all' card in the life world an optional `examples_life` override, used when S.world==='life'. Start with: will-gap-paid-to-play-reveal prompt -> 'You knit scarves for fun. A neighbour's shop pays you per scarf for a month, then stops ordering. Compared with people never paid, people in your position later knit...'; self-efficacy-choice scenario -> 'Your friend dreads speaking at the residents' meeting or a family gathering...'; reversible-doors-swipe 'Getting a face tattoo' -> 'Selling the family home'; doomscroll-loop-no-ending 'Opening card packs in a game' -> 'Scratch cards at the newsagent'; self-reflection-loop-example step 1 -> 'Your choir's concert went well, but you came in late twice...'.

issues.problem: The result makes me do the app's job. Will 10, Skill 5, Open door 5, and the text says: 'Look at your lowest score above: if it's Skill, do one...; if it's the Open door... If they tie, start with...'. That is a decision tree printed as a paragraph, when the app already knows my scores. The plot dot also sits on the 'Will' label, so the screenshot shows 'W●'. The card then switches from 'Open door' to 'Opportunity' in the model and Try today, which is confusing.
issues.fix: Compute the lowest axis in the renderer and fill it in: 'Your weakest pillar today: {label} ({score}/10). Next move: {action}', with action = Skill -> 'one 5-minute practice rep', Open door -> 'ask one person for the time or the chance this week', Will -> 'write one sentence on why this matters to you'. On a tie, say 'Open door and Skill tie; start with the Open door: one ask is the cheapest move.' Move the axis labels outside the circles, or keep the dot at least 24px from any label. Use 'Open door' everywhere: model -> 'Stuck? Don't push everywhere. Find the missing pillar: Will, Skill or Open door.'; try_today -> '...rate Will, Skill and Open door out of 10...'.

issues.problem: Korzybski's point is that a map can mislead about the territory. It is a caution about accuracy, not a licence to put truth second. The model 'Ask "useful for what?" before asking "true or false?"' gets the order backwards. Coming two cards before the pragmatism card, the feed slides toward 'whatever works is true'. A thoughtful reader will object, and a young one may absorb it. The reveal also flatters the wrong answer: 'If you picked the photo, you spotted the catch'.
issues.fix: Model -> 'Every belief is a map. Ask where it's accurate, and what trip it was drawn for.' Reveal -> 'For most trips, the tube map wins: it bends geography on purpose so you can act fast. But the bending has a cost. Studies of London riders found the distortions push some onto slower routes, even riding between stops that are quicker to walk. A map is only as good as the trip it was built for.'

issues.problem: The reveal credits Lally (2010) with more than she found. Her study showed that one missed day did not measurably slow habit formation. It did not show that 'the long gap after is the real risk'; that is Clear's extrapolation, presented here as data. The insight repeats the same blur. ''Monday' turns one miss into four' is cute but only true midweek.
issues.fix: Reveal -> 'The second. In Lally's 2010 habit study, missing a single day didn't measurably set people back. The study didn't test long gaps, but waiting for "Monday" can turn one miss into several. Doubling up sounds keen, but it makes tomorrow heavier. Tiny today wins.' Insight -> 'A miss is an event, not a verdict about you. Lally's 2010 study found one missed day barely slowed habit forming. "Never miss twice" is Clear's rule of thumb built on that.'

issues.problem: The card is filed under 'expected value', but it never teaches expected value: no probabilities, no weighing of payoffs. It teaches Duke's 'resulting', which is a fine lesson under a misleading label. The 'Why' link and the Map will tell me I've learned EV when I haven't.
issues.fix: Either change concept to 'resulting' (title stays), or add a third step: scenario 'A 10% chance of losing £50, or a sure £3 fee for insurance on a £50 item. Which is the better bet on average?' Options: 'Skip the insurance: on average it costs £5, the fee £3' (best? no) / 'Pay the £3: on average the risk costs £5, more than the fee' (best: true, feedback 'Right: 10% × £50 = £5 expected loss. Weigh chance times stakes, then decide.'). Then add to insight: 'Expected value is the tool: chance times stakes, summed.'

issues.problem: The card cites David Allen's Getting Things Done for a different rule. Allen's two-minute rule means 'if a task takes under two minutes, do it now', not 'shrink a habit to a two-minute start'. Putting both under one name is the kind of sloppiness that makes a careful reader doubt the rest.
issues.fix: Change source.thinkers to ['James Clear', 'BJ Fogg'] and source.work to 'Clear, Atomic Habits (2018); Fogg, Tiny Habits (2019)'. Or keep Allen and add to the insight: 'Not to be confused with David Allen's rule: if it takes under two minutes, do it now.'

issues.problem: The Aristotle quote is accurate, but it is about virtue formed through habit (character), not belief in one's ability. Placed under Bandura with no comment, it makes Aristotle sound like a self-efficacy theorist. The link is real but needs one honest sentence. The same small stretch applies to Seneca's 'begun to be a friend to myself' (Hecato) on the self-compassion card.
issues.fix: Add a `from_source.note` field (or append to next_read) for self-efficacy-choice: 'Aristotle is talking about character, not confidence, but the mechanism rhymes: we become by doing.' For self-compassion-lookalike-swipe: 'For Seneca, being one's own friend meant living by reason, a sterner kindness than today's word.'

personas.verdict: Better than I expected. These cards respect evidence. The lottery card corrects its own 1978 study with the 2020 Swedish data. The mindset card admits its effects are small. The pragmatism card names Russell's objection. The quotations from Seneca, Mill, Confucius, Aristotle and James are accurate and come with real next readings, which as a teacher I value most. Nothing shamed me, and the pause card every eight cards is a decent answer to the doomscroll irony. Where it falls short of depth: it sometimes trades accuracy for neatness (Lally overstated, Allen conflated, EV mislabelled, the map model putting usefulness ahead of truth). The 'Everyday life' world still dresses everything for a sixteen-year-old in trainers. The 'Next' button even breaks my world choice. The 30-second games are pleasant but rarely gripping. I would come back for the quotations and the honest reveals, not for the play. A solid 7 on substance, 6 on delight.

personas.persona: Sam, 24, a recent graduate dealing with anxiety and low self-worth after a rough year. I chose the "Everyday life" world. I'm sensitive to anything that shames me, labels me or pushes me, and I need the app to feel safe and actually useful.

issues.problem: I'm a graduate coming off a bad year. The first thing this card says is that adults' biggest life regret is school, which lands on exactly my sore spot. The card isn't marked sensitive, so it has no 'reflection, not diagnosis' / helpline footer (screenshot -b confirms there isn't one). The insight also opens with 'Verdict:', the word every other card promises it isn't giving.
issues.fix: Set "sensitive": true. Change the hook to "What do adults regret most? Guess how big a share is about school." In insight, replace "Verdict: regret follows open doors, at 16 or 46." with "Takeaway: regret follows open doors, at 16 or 46, and education is one of the doors that stays open longest." Add to the end of explain: " If school already feels like a closed chapter, that's the hopeful part: courses, re-sits and late starts are common."

issues.problem: On swipe cards, the results list puts an orange X next to every item I sorted wrong ('Belongs in: Look-alike'). On self-compassion-lookalike-swipe-a I got three orange X's in a row on a card about being kind to myself. It reads like a marked exam and I felt scolded.
issues.fix: On cards with sensitive:true, replace the X/check icons with neutral side tags ('Look-alike' / 'Self-compassion' pills in the axis colour), and change the 'Belongs in:' prefix to 'Often counts as:'. Keep the X/check only on non-sensitive cards.

issues.problem: 'I'll skip practice for the rest of the month. I deserve it.' gets a flat 'look-alike'. If someone is actually burnt out, a long break can be the kind choice, so the card risks teaching that resting is self-indulgent. The hook also starts from suspicion ('just a nicer word for making excuses?').
issues.fix: Change that item's why to: "Depends on the reason. If you're burnt out, a planned break is real care. If it's to avoid the sting, a short rest plus a restart date is kinder." Change the hook to: "Being kind to yourself after a fail: excuse, or the thing that gets you back up?"

issues.problem: My result was 'Leaning fixed today (on these topics)', in big underlined headline type next to a slider sitting near 'Fixed'. The 'snapshot, not a verdict' line is there, but it's small and grey. On a card the app itself rates 'contested', the label still feels like a judgement on me, and the slider shows nothing to try.
issues.fix: Rename the first zone's label to "Today, hard things feel personal" and change its text to: "Your answers treat hard things as tests of who you are. That's tiring, very common, and often what a rough patch does, not a fixed trait. Next time, test the method instead: 'which part lost me?'" Make the 'A snapshot of today's answers, not a verdict on you.' line the same size and colour as the body text.

issues.problem: The card's message is 'keep the lesson, drop the shame', but the Confucius quote ('To have faults and not to reform them... should be pronounced having faults') is a stern judgement, and it sits right above my try-today. For me it brought the shame back in.
issues.fix: Replace from_source.quote with "When you have faults, do not fear to abandon them." and set cite to "Confucius, Analects I.8 (trans. James Legge, 1861)" and next_read to "Analects, Book I.8 and XV.29".

issues.problem: try_today ('Pick one past choice you regret...') invites rumination for someone anxious, and there's no limit on how big a regret to pick. The card is sensitive and shows the footer, but the task itself has no safety rail.
issues.fix: Change try_today to: "Pick one small past choice that still bugs you (not the biggest one). Ask: given what I knew then, was it reasonable? Write one sentence, then close the note."

issues.problem: This card is about a limiting belief about myself ('not a people person') and asks me to start a chat with someone every day for a week. That's a real stretch for anxious people. Yet it isn't marked sensitive (no footer), and it gives no easier option.
issues.fix: Set "sensitive": true. Change choice 3 to "For one week, try one tiny chat a day (even 'thanks, have a good one') and note how each goes". Append to try_today: " Pick the smallest version that still counts."

issues.problem: I picked 'Everyday life', but a lot of the copy is about school (speaking up in class, revising, 'a talk at school', phones in schools). The feed screenshot shows a 'since age 11 / chips after school' card. At 24 it makes me feel the app isn't meant for me.
issues.fix: For audience 'all' cards in the Everyday-life world, pair every school example with an adult one: e.g. self-efficacy-choice scenario → "...dreads speaking up in meetings, class or at family dinners..."; wso-triad-venn prompt list → "(job applications, an instrument, getting fitter, a side project)". Filter cards whose copy assumes school age (like the memento-mori school-friends card) out of the Everyday-life world.

personas.verdict: Mostly it felt kind. Lines like "a miss is an event, not a verdict", "replaying isn't reviewing" and "one slip is one data point" actually helped me, and the tiny try-todays are things I can do on a bad day. What held it back was small moments of feeling judged: three orange X's on the self-compassion card, a bold 'Leaning fixed' headline, a stern Confucius quote on the 'drop the shame' card, and a regret card about school with no safety footer, which is rough for a struggling graduate. Fix those and add more adult examples, and I'd keep scrolling and maybe share the never-miss-twice card.

personas.persona: Dr. Okafor, 51, research psychologist. Checks every claim, attribution and effect size; hunts for replication-crisis myths, overclaiming and bad survey design. Played the "Everyday life" feed (20 cards, session 12). Looked at 11 screenshots: growth-mindset a/b, wso-triad a/b, regret b, hedonic a, never-miss a, useful-truth a, pigeons b, will-gap a, view-map-dark.

issues.problem: Every reveal card gives a player who picks a 'wrong' answer the heading 'Here's what the research found.' (app.js line 556), even on cards marked evidence 'philosophy'. On useful-truth-people-person the screenshot shows that heading above a passage about Peirce and James, which is philosophy, not research. On map-territory-subway-reveal the heading sits above an intuition argument. The interface turns opinions into findings, which is exactly the overclaiming the cards' own caveats try to avoid.
issues.fix: In the reveal game at app.js:556, pick the heading by card.evidence: 'strong' or 'moderate' -> "Here's what the research found."; 'contested' -> "Here's what studies suggest (still debated)."; 'philosophy' -> "Here's the idea." Pass card.evidence into the reveal function (it already receives card).

issues.problem: The scale is poorly built. (1) The options are always listed from fixed to growth and the marker moves live, so the 'good' answer is obvious, social desirability takes over, and the scale measures who can spot the right answer. (2) Scoring is unbalanced: Q2 runs -2/0/1/2 with no -1, and Q3 runs -2/0/2. A fixed-leaning player can't land in the middle, and the zone cut-offs differ from item to item. (3) Q4 marks the most self-aware answer, 'Easy when I'm drained, stretch when I have energy', BELOW 'Take the stretch' (1 vs 2), and gives 'Depends on who's watching', a performance-goal answer, a neutral 0. (4) Q2 'It stings, but I'm curious how they got there' (1) and 'I wonder how they practise' (2) say almost the same thing. (5) Q4's stem says 'you usually…' but the options read as answers to a different question ('The easy one.').
issues.fix: Give every item 4 options scored -2,-1,1,2 and drop the neutral 'Depends' answers, or keep 5 options with a real -1. Q2: change 'Some of it is talent, some is practice.' to value -1 and replace 'I wonder how they practise' with 'I ask them what their practice looks like.' (2). issues.problem: The card attributes to Lally et al. (2010) something the study did not test. Lally reported that missing one opportunity did not materially affect habit formation. The study did not show that 'the long gap after is the real risk', and nothing in it supports ''Monday' turns one miss into four' or the claim about doubling up. It was also a small sample (96 people recruited, fewer analysed, and a good model fit for only about 39). The card dresses Clear's rule of thumb up as a finding.
issues.fix: Reveal: "The second. In a small 2010 study (Lally and colleagues, about 80 people), missing a single day didn't measurably slow habit forming. The study didn't test long gaps, but common sense says a run of misses makes restarting harder. 'Monday' can turn one miss into four, and doubling up makes tomorrow heavier. Tiny today is the safe bet." Insight: replace 'the long gap after is the risk' with 'longer gaps weren't tested'.

issues.problem: The reveal argues that memories and friends' views are 'filtered through the belief itself', but the winning option ('see how each goes') is judged by the same biased person. That is the confirmation-bias problem again, unsolved. 'Ask three friends' isn't filtered by YOUR belief either. The experiment has no outcome criterion, so it can't show the belief is false. The hook 'How would you prove that?' asks for proof, but the game rewards falsification.
issues.fix: Change choice 3 to 'For one week, start one short chat a day and note one fact each time: did they ask me something back?'. Change the hook to "'I'm just not a people person.' How would you test that?" Rewrite the first reveal sentence as: "Memory is selective, and the belief keeps you out of the moments that would test it. Friends help, but a small experiment with a clear check beats both." Keep the Peirce and James lines.

issues.problem: The effect size is reported well (about d = -0.34), but the scenario stretches the evidence. Deci, Koestner & Ryan (1999) measured free-choice play over a few minutes, usually within one lab session. The card describes a month of paid work and 'later' behaviour, which those studies do not cover. 'Praise helped adults more than children' is also slightly off: in the meta-analysis, verbal rewards raised free-choice behaviour for college students but not for children.
issues.fix: Prompt: "You make video edits for fun. In a lab-style setup, you're paid per edit for a session, then the pay stops and you're left alone with free time. Compared with people never paid, people like you go on to make…". In the reveal, change 'praise helped adults more than children' to 'praise raised later play in college students but not in children'. Add 'Most studies were short lab sessions; long-run effects at work are less clear' to the insight.

issues.problem: The model line 'Random rewards build the stickiest habits' overgeneralises Ferster & Skinner. Their finding is the partial-reinforcement extinction effect: behaviour rewarded intermittently holds out longer once rewards stop. It is not a claim that random rewards form habits faster or more strongly. Today's habit research (e.g. Wood) treats habit as cue-driven automaticity, a separate idea. The card is also marked 'strong' while also saying in effect 'feeds are slot machines', and that analogy carries no evidence.
issues.fix: Model: 'Random rewards make a behaviour the hardest to stop when the rewards dry up. Make the good stuff predictable and the feed boring.' Reveal, last sentence: 'Some app features (pull to refresh, loot packs) borrow the same random-payout design, though how much they hook people is still studied.'

issues.problem: The reveal cites 'studies of London riders found the map's distortions push some people onto slower routes', but the source field lists only Korzybski and Box, so nobody can check the claim. The finding is Guo (2011). Separately, the hook says 'You're lost in London', while the prompt is about getting across fast, so the two frames differ.
issues.fix: Add to source.work: "Guo, 'Mind the map! The impact of transit maps on path choice in public transit', Transportation Research Part A (2011)" and add 'Zhan Guo' to thinkers. Change the reveal to '…a study of London riders (Guo, 2011) found…'. Hook: 'You need to cross London fast. Satellite photo or tube map?'

issues.problem: The card mixes up attributions. David Allen's two-minute rule (GTD) means 'if a task takes under two minutes, do it now'. That is a different rule from Clear's 'shrink a new habit to a two-minute start'. 'Shoes on makes the walk or run likely' is also stated as fact without support.
issues.fix: In source.work, change to 'Clear, Atomic Habits (2018); Fogg, Tiny Habits (2019)' and remove David Allen from thinkers, or add '(Allen's rule is different: do any task under 2 minutes now)'. Change that item's why to: 'Starting is the hard part. Shoes on makes the run easier to begin.'

personas.verdict: Overall, this is a careful feed, better than most pop-psych content. Effect sizes appear where they matter (Deci's d of about -0.34). The growth-mindset caveats match Sisk 2018 and Yeager 2019. The hedonic card correctly updates Brickman with Lindqvist 2020. Regret shares match Roese & Summerville, and WSO is honestly labelled 'not a validated scale'. My main complaints are about overclaiming at the edges. A generic 'Here's what the research found' heading appears on philosophy cards. Some study-attributed claims go beyond what the studies showed (Lally on long gaps, Ferster & Skinner on 'stickiest habits', Deci stretched to a month of paid work). The weakest instrument is the growth-mindset spectrum: transparent order, unbalanced scoring, and the most self-aware answer scored below the textbook one. Fix those and I would rate usefulness and safety an 8. Fun stays at about 6 for me, because the many reveal cards with an obvious correct answer feel like quizzes rather than games.

issues.problem: The reveal heading says 'Here's what the research found.', but this card is evidence: philosophy (Peirce and James), not a study. The same generic heading appears on map-territory (a philosophy card). It overclaims, and that undermines trust in the cards that do cite real research.
issues.fix: In app.js, pick the reveal heading by evidence level: strong/moderate → 'Here's what the research found.'; philosophy → 'Here's the idea.'; contested → 'Here's what studies suggest (it's debated).' Also trim the reveal to: 'Memories and friends' opinions are filtered through the belief itself. Pragmatists like Peirce and James said: test an idea by what happens when you act on it. So act as if it might be false, and watch.'

issues.problem: The 'correct' answer (About the same) rests on a 22-person 1978 study, and the reveal then says the large 2020 Swedish study found winners stayed more satisfied for years. Players who picked 'Clearly happier' get marked wrong for the answer the better evidence partly supports. That feels unfair, and an unfair answer kills replay. The hook also says 'a year on' while the prompt says 'up to about 18 months'.
issues.fix: Change the prompt to: 'Lottery winners rated how much they enjoyed everyday moments (a chat, a joke, breakfast). Compared with their neighbours, the winners enjoyed them…', with choices ['More', 'About the same or a bit less', 'Much less'] and answer 1. Change the hook to: 'You win the lottery. Does breakfast taste better a year later?' Keep the Swedish life-satisfaction finding in the reveal as the twist.

issues.problem: The hook ('You're lost in London') contradicts the game. If you're lost on the street, the satellite photo really is the better tool. The prompt then switches to 'get across London fast', so the 'right' answer feels like a trick.

issues.problem: The prompt repeats the hook almost word for word right under it (two pigeons, every peck, random), so the first screen reads the same thing twice and wastes the 30 seconds. The reveal also speaks only to people who picked A, so a player who picked 'About the same' (as in the screenshot) gets no feedback on their choice.
issues.fix: Change the prompt to: 'Then the food stops completely. Which pigeon keeps pecking longer?' and let the hook carry the setup. Change the reveal's second sentence to: 'Picked A or "same"? Natural guess: more food should mean a stronger habit. But random rewards are much harder to give up (Ferster & Skinner).'

issues.problem: After a wrong answer on step 2, a large heading 'Here's another way to play it.' appears directly above THE MODEL box. It reads as if a new mini-game is starting, not a takeaway, and I looked for something to tap.
issues.fix: On choice cards, replace that heading with 'The takeaway' (or drop it entirely so THE MODEL box stands alone).

personas.verdict: The writing is warm and careful, and the try-today actions are concrete and easy to do. It never shames me, and the hedging on evidence is honest. That's where the 9 on safety comes from. As a game it feels more like a well-written quiz than a 30-second toy. Getting an answer right is just a colour change, the swipe cards have no score, and the long reveals push the payoff below the fold. The feed also repeated itself: two doomscroll cards in a row, and the 'I'm not a ___ person' line four times. That kills the 'one more' pull. If you fix the reward moment, the spacing between similar cards and the few cards that feel unfair or confusing (hedonic adaptation, the map hook, the Venn overlap), I'd score fun and hook 8. Right now I'd play the next card, but I wouldn't share one yet.
